title: Chapter 5 – Teeth in the Ferns
html:
Grandfather allows it, in the end, on one condition.

"Within arm's reach," he says to Su Qinghe, in the main hall, with the whole family pretending not to listen. "Every moment. If you lose sight of him, you come home."

"Yes, Father."

"And you stay in the outer forest. Not past the second ridge."

"Yes, Father."

He looks at his daughter-in-law for a long moment, and then at the small boy standing beside her in a short robe two sizes too big. "Bring me back a mist rabbit," he says. "I haven't eaten one in years."

Lin Feng does not speak to his brother for three days.

He is thirteen now, at the fourth layer, a head taller than any of the other cousins, and he was not allowed past the eastern terraces until he was ten. He says none of this out loud. He does not need to. He simply stops sitting beside Lin Jian at meals, and when they pass in the courtyard he looks at a point a little above his brother's head, and in the evenings he trains alone in the gate yard with his borrowed spear until Fourth Uncle comes out and tells him to stop before he puts his own eye out.

Lin Jian understands. In Lin Feng's place, he would feel the same. He also knows there is nothing he can say about it that would help, so he says nothing, and on the first warm morning of spring he walks out of the gate behind his mother and does not look back.

\ \ \*

The winter has not been idle.

He has spent it with Uncle Mao in the courtyard, learning his second art. The Five-Element Ward Art he practices every day, until the shimmer over a scrape comes in half the time it did in autumn and the panel's efficiency figure creeps up to thirty-four percent. But Uncle Mao's own root is earth, and earth is what the old man teaches best, and when the snow is deepest he sets the children to learning Earthen Rampart.

"The ground is the oldest shield there is," Uncle Mao says. "You don't make the wall. You ask the earth to stand up."

Lin Bo can raise a wall to his waist. Lin Hu, to his knees. Lin Feng, when he deigns to attend, can raise a slab of frozen earth as high as his own shoulders and hold it long enough to stop a thrown log. Lin Jian, feeding the earth gate of his wheel through the seals one element at a time, can raise a ridge of soil about as high as his own shin.

Lin Hu finds this very funny.

Lin Jian does not mind. A shin-high ridge, raised at the right place at the right moment, is a trip wire. He has spent the winter practicing raising it fast, not high.

\ \ \*

The outer mountains begin an hour's walk east of the terraces, past the last rice field, across a stream on stepping stones, and up a slope where the pines give way to something older.

Lin Jian stops at the top of the slope and stares.

The trees are enormous. Cedars as broad as the gatehouse, their bark furrowed like the skin of old elephants, rising a hundred feet before the first branch. Pines with trunks so thick that three men could not link arms around them. Oaks, broad-leaved and black-barked, their roots heaving up out of the ground like the backs of sleeping animals. The light comes down through the canopy in long green shafts, thick with drifting pollen, and the air smells of resin and wet earth and something he does not have a word for.

And the Qi.

On the hill it is a draft. Here it is a current. He feels it press against his skin, cool and rich and slightly strange, as if the ground under the forest is breathing out.

"There are veins under the mountains," his mother says, beside him. "Dozens. Hundreds. Nobody knows how many. Most of them too deep to tap, or too small to fight over, or too dangerous to reach." She settles her pack on her shoulders. "That's why the beasts are here. They feed on it, the way we do. The deeper you go, the richer the veins, and the stronger the beasts. Out here, first rank, a few second. Past the second ridge, the middle mountains, it's second and third. Past that," she nods eastward, where blue peaks rise above the trees like teeth, "the inner range. Fourth rank. Fifth. Beasts with cores in their skulls the size of your fist, and minds as sharp as yours or mine."

"Have you been there?"

"Once." She does not say anything else, and he does not ask.

She is dressed for the forest the way he has never seen her dressed at home: a gray short robe of quilted hemp, close-fitting leggings tucked into soft boots, her hair bound tightly at the nape of her neck. A knife sheathed horizontally across the small of her back. No bow; she gave up the bow, she tells him, the year she reached the third layer.

"A bow is for people who can't throw water," she says.

She shows him. She lifts two fingers toward a knot in the trunk of a cedar twenty paces away, and makes a short, sharp seal with her other hand, and a thread of water leaps from her fingertips, thin as a knitting needle, faster than he can follow. There is a crack. A neat hole appears in the bark, the size of his thumb, and water drips from it.

"Tidal Spear," she says. "It doesn't look like much. It doesn't need to. A thrown spear is heavy. A thrown needle is fast." She looks at him. "Which one would you rather be hit by?"

Lin Jian looks at the hole in the cedar, and at the water still dripping from the tree, and does a quick calculation of mass and velocity and cross-sectional area, and says nothing at all, because what he is thinking is: She doesn't know it, but she has just described a pressure jet.

"Can you teach me?"

"No." She says it without hesitation. "Not yet. Tidal Spear wants the fourth layer at least, and a water root with some depth to it. Yours is thin, and you are not there yet." She glances at him sideways. "As far as anyone knows."

"And when I do?"

His mother considers him for a moment, the way she considers a trail before she steps onto it. "When you do," she says, "we'll see what your five elements make of it. A five-element root can throw water, they say, at half the strength and twice the labor. I've never seen one heal a scrape on the first day, either." She turns and starts up the slope. "Keep up."

He keeps up.

\ \ \*

She teaches him the forest the way her father taught her: by walking it.

"Blood-stop grass," she says, crouching by a stream bank and parting a clump of narrow leaves with red edges. "Chew it and pack it in a wound and the bleeding slows. Your aunt pays a stone for a basketful." He touches a leaf, and scans it, and his head swims.

```
[Scan: Blood-Stop Grass]
Active compounds: coagulant glycosides, trace Qi (wood)
Creation Energy +2 (41 / 100)
```

"Frostbell moss," she says, an hour later, on the north face of a boulder where the snow still lingers in the shadows. Pale green cushions, cold to the touch, studded with tiny white flowers like frozen bells. "Grows only where the sun never reaches. Your aunt makes fever pills from it. It stores water Qi the way a jar stores rain."

```
[Scan: Frostbell Moss]
Structure: crystalline water-element Qi storage in cell walls
Creation Energy +3 (44 / 100)
```

Iron-root vine, which climbs the oaks in ropes as thick as his wrist and bleeds a sap that burns like pepper. A shy gray creature at the edge of a clearing that his mother calls a mist rabbit, which sits up on its hind legs, looks at them with enormous black eyes, and then blurs and vanishes into a puff of vapor before he can blink.

"First rank," his mother says. "They're harmless. They're also delicious, and impossible to catch, which is why your grandfather wants one." She shakes her head. "The old man is teasing me."

They walk. They eat cold rice balls on a fallen log in a shaft of sunlight. His mother talks more than he has ever heard her talk, in a low, even voice, about the forest and its moods: which birds go silent before a predator, which paths the deer use, why you never drink from a still pool in the Beast Mountains.

Then, when they have been sitting quietly on the log for a while, she says, without changing her tone at all, "My father brought me here when I was ten."

Lin Jian waits.

"He was a rogue cultivator. Like his father. We had no hill. No clan. Just the mountains, and the money we could make from them." She looks at the trees. "When I was twelve, a fourth-rank beast killed him a day's walk east of here. I buried him under a cedar. I could show you the tree." She is quiet for a moment. "The mountains give, Jian. They give everything. And they take."

He does not know what to say. He puts his hand on her arm, and she lets it stay there.

Then she stands up, brushes off her leggings, and points across the valley with her chin.

On the far ridge, perhaps half a mile away, a line of gray shapes is moving through the trees in single file. Six of them. Even at this distance he can see that they are big, bigger than any dog, and that the fur along their spines lies in dark, overlapping plates like roof tiles.

"Iron-backed wolves," his mother says. "The same kind your founder drove off the hill. That's a hunting pack. They are out of the middle mountains: the winter was hard, and they have followed the deer down. The leader is first rank, peak tier, as strong as a ninth-layer cultivator. The rest are low and medium." She looks down at him. "We have been under the Still Water Veil since the stream, and so have you, and we are downwind. To them we are two stones on a log. Close your eyes. Don't look at them. Feel for them."

He closes his eyes. At first there is only the forest: the slow, cool breathing of the trees, the tiny bright sparks of birds, the sleepy warmth of his mother beside him. Then, far off, he finds them. Six points of pressure moving in a line. Five of them are like the boar would be, if he had felt for it: dull and heavy, like warm stones. The sixth is different. It is sharper. Denser. It presses on the edge of his attention like a thumb.

"The one in front," he says. "It feels heavier."

"That's rank." His mother sounds satisfied. "Everything that cultivates has a weight. A first-rank beast weighs about what a Qi Refining cultivator does, tier for tier. A second-rank beast weighs what a Foundation does: you'll feel it from farther away, and it will feel you back. If something feels as heavy as your grandfather, you don't wait to find out what it is. You leave." She watches the pack disappear over the ridge. "A hard winter is the only reason they are this far out. They will go back up when the snow melts. Still. We tell your grandfather tonight." She shoulders her pack. "Let's not sit in one place too long. Come on. There's a stand of iron-root by the stream I want to show you."

And the moment is gone.

\ \ \*

They hear the boar before they see it.

It is a sound like a cart being dragged through brush: snapping, crashing, a deep, wet grunting that seems to come from the ground itself. Then, fifty paces away through the ferns, something enormous lifts its head.

It is the size of a draft horse. Its back bristles with a ridge of horn-bone spines as long as his forearm, and two tusks curve up from its lower jaw, yellowed and chipped, each one as long as a sword. It stands chest-deep in the ferns, its small eyes fixed on them, and its breath steams in the cool air.

"Thornback boar," his mother says, very quietly. She has not moved. Neither has he. "First rank, medium tier. Four hundred kilos. Don't run."

He does not run. He looks at it, and something in his mind shifts gear, the way it always has when a problem arrives. Mass. Velocity. Turning radius. He notices that it holds its head slightly to the right. He notices that its left eye is not black, like its right. It is clouded and milky white.

"It's blind on the left," he says.

His mother's eyes flick to the boar, and back. "Yes."

The boar lowers its head and charges.

It covers the first twenty paces in the time it takes him to draw breath. The ground shakes. The ferns part before it like water. His mother's hand comes up, two fingers extended, and a thread of water cracks out of them and strikes the boar's shoulder, and it does not even slow down. Its hide is thick, and the spines on its back shed the water like rain off a roof.

"Jian, behind me," she says.

He does not go behind her. He has already done the arithmetic. If he goes behind her, the boar hits both of them.

He runs to the left, toward the biggest cedar in the clearing, a trunk as broad as a doorway, and stops in front of it, facing the boar, and waits.

The boar swings toward him. It is faster than anything that size should be. Fifteen paces. Ten. He can smell it: wet hide and rot and musk. Five paces. He can see the cracks in its tusks.

He throws himself to the left. Into the blind side.

The boar does not see him go. It sees the cedar, too late, and tries to turn, and four hundred kilos of momentum do not turn. Its right shoulder smashes into the trunk with a sound like a thunderclap. Bark explodes. The whole tree shudders to its crown, and a rain of needles and dead twigs comes down over the clearing.

The boar staggers. Shakes its massive head. Turns, slowly, groggily, to find him.

He is on his knees in the ferns three paces to its left, his hands already moving through the earth seals, one element, then the next, the way he has practiced all winter. He feeds everything he has into the last gate.

A ridge of soil and roots bursts up out of the ground under the boar's left foreleg. It is only shin-high. It does not need to be any higher.

The boar steps forward, onto nothing, and its leg folds. Its whole weight pitches sideways. For one moment it is down on its shoulder in the ferns, its throat exposed, its legs churning for purchase.

The air around his mother turns cold.

He sees frost spread across the ferns in a ring around the boar like a breath on a window. The boar's churning legs slow, stiffen, crusted white. Moonlit Glacier, he will learn later. A water art, the ice side of it. Then his mother's hand comes up again, two fingers straight as a blade, and three threads of water crack out one after another, so fast they make a single sound, and strike the boar in the same place, low on its neck, under the jaw, where the spines do not reach.

The first opens the hide. The second goes into the hole the first made. The third goes deeper.

The boar screams, a high, terrible sound, and thrashes, and then it is still.

Lin Jian sits in the ferns with his hands in the dirt and finds that he is shaking so hard his teeth rattle.

His mother walks over, steps around the steaming body of the boar, crouches in front of him, and takes his face in both hands. Her fingers are icy. She looks into his eyes for a long moment.

"Are you hurt?"

"No."

"Why didn't you get behind me?"

"It would have hit both of us," he says. His voice is very small. "It ran straight. Big things can't turn fast. And it couldn't see on one side. So I stood in front of the tree. And then I," he swallows, "I made it trip."

His mother says nothing. She looks at the cedar, at the long white scar where the bark has been torn away, and at the shin-high ridge of earth, already crumbling, beside the boar's left foreleg. And she looks at him.

"My father taught me that," she says at last. "The tree. It took him three years." She lets go of his face. "He never taught me the other part. Where did you learn to raise a wall that fast?"

"Uncle Mao. I practiced all winter."

"Fast," she says. "Not high."

"High wasn't the point."

His mother looks at him a moment longer. Then she laughs, suddenly, a short, startled sound, and pulls him against her shoulder and holds him there while the shaking goes out of him.

\ \ \*

She butchers the boar where it lies, quickly and expertly, with the knife from the small of her back. The meat they will leave for the forest; it is too much to carry and too far to drag. The tusks, the spines and the hide they will take. The tusks alone will sell for twenty stones in Willow Ford. The spines are worth more to a talisman maker.

While she works, Lin Jian sits beside the boar's head with his hand on its cooling hide, and scans.

```
[Scan: Thornback Boar (First Rank, Deceased)]
Structure: Qi-reinforced keratin spines, dense dermal layer, enlarged adrenal analog
Note: No beast core present (first-rank beasts do not condense cores)
Creation Energy +6 (50 / 100)
```

Halfway. After six years, halfway.

He sits with that for a moment, his hand on the rough, cooling hide. Six years of cloth and rice and feathers and stolen moments at the tribute chest, a point or two at a time. And one morning in the forest has given him fourteen. The hill has been scanned nearly bare. Out here, every fern and stone and animal is something he has never touched.

He looks east, at the blue teeth of the inner range, and understands for the first time why his mother came back to these mountains for ten years, and why her father died in them.

When they start home, late in the afternoon, the pack on his mother's back is heavy with tusks and spines, and a mist rabbit hangs limp from her belt. She has caught it on the way back, so fast he did not see her move. "For your grandfather," she says. "So he'll stop teasing me."

They walk in silence through the long gold light. At the stream, where the stepping stones cross back toward the terraces, she stops and looks down at him.

"Whatever you are, Jian," she says, "you need a teacher."

He looks up at her.

"Not your Uncle Mao. He's a good man and a good teacher, and what he knows, he's teaching you already. I mean someone who can teach you the things your hands want to learn." She looks at his hands. They are scratched and filthy and still trembling slightly. "And someone who won't ask too many questions."

"Do you know someone like that?"

His mother is quiet for a long time.

"There's a man two valleys east," she says at last. "He mends farm tools for the villages and drinks most of what they pay him. He has one arm." She looks toward the east, where the mountains are turning purple in the evening light. "Fifteen years ago, he was the finest artifact refiner I ever met. Next month, when we take the tusks to Willow Ford, we'll go a little out of our way."

She steps out onto the first stone.

"His name," she says, over her shoulder, "is Hu. And whatever you do, don't let him see you looking at his arm."

She does not say anything else, all the way home.

\ \ \*

The family meets them at the gate.

Word has gone ahead. Some farmer on the last terrace has seen them coming down the slope with a pack full of tusks, and by the time they reach the gate road half the household is in the yard. Fourth Uncle's guards crowd round to look at the spines. Third Aunt pushes through them, takes the basket of blood-stop grass and frostbell moss off Lin Jian's back, inspects it with professional suspicion, and announces that it is the best-cut blood-stop she has seen in a year and she will pay him two stones for it out of the pill-room money, and he is not to tell his cousins. Grandfather accepts the mist rabbit from his daughter-in-law's hand with grave ceremony, as though it were a tribute from a neighboring prince, and then spoils it by grinning like a boy.

"Within arm's reach?" he asks.

"Every moment, Father," says Su Qinghe, and does not mention the boar at all.

She does not need to. Old Gou, who has been looking at the tusks, has already measured them against his own forearm and whistled, and by dinner the story has gone round the household three times and grown with each telling. By the third, the boar is as big as an ox, and Su Qinghe has killed it with a single stroke, and Lin Jian has climbed a tree. He does not correct anyone. It is a much better story for him than the true one.

Lin Feng is not at dinner.

Lin Jian finds out where he is after the lamps are out, when the door of their room slides open and his brother comes in from the gate yard, smelling of sweat and cold air, and sits down heavily on the edge of his own bedroll without lighting the lamp.

For a while neither of them says anything.

"Old Gou says it was a thornback," Lin Feng says at last, to the dark. "Four hundred kilos."

"About that."

"He says Mother put three water darts in the same hole."

"She did."

Silence. Then, grudgingly: "Did you climb a tree?"

Lin Jian considers the question. He could say yes. It would be the end of it. Lin Feng would snort and roll over and in the morning things would be as they were.

"No," he says. "I stood in front of one."

Lin Feng turns his head. In the faint moonlight from the window, Lin Jian can see the shape of his face, and the expression on it, which is not the one he expects.

"It was blind on the left," Lin Jian says. "So I made it run at the tree, and then I jumped to the blind side. It hit the tree. Then I raised a ridge under its foot. Earthen Rampart. It fell over, and Mother killed it."

"Your ridge is the height of a radish."

"It doesn't need to be high. It needs to be fast, and in the right place." He hesitates. "It's the same with your fire ring. You make it big. If you made it small and fast, under someone's feet, they'd have to jump. And while they're jumping, they can't do anything else."

Lin Feng is silent for so long that Lin Jian thinks he has fallen asleep sitting up.

Then his brother lies down, pulls his blanket up to his chin, and says to the ceiling, "Show me tomorrow. In the gate yard. Before Uncle Mao gets up."

"All right."

"And if you tell anyone I asked you, radish, I'll put you in the koi pond."

"All right."

Lin Feng turns on his side, away from him. A minute later, very quietly, he says, "I'm glad you didn't die."

Then he is asleep, or pretending to be, and Lin Jian lies awake in the dark, thinking about a one-armed man two valleys east, and about how his mother said his name as if she were setting down something heavy.

Hu, he thinks. Don't look at his arm.
